newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.

text.p: By Peter Campbell*
OLYMPIC SAILING ON SYDNEY HARBOUR

Sailing will become a focal point of the Sydney 2000 Olympics following the decision by the International Sailing Federation (ISAF) to adopt an innovative plan put forward by the Sydney organising committee at the ISAF annual conference in Brighton, England, last week.

Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games (SOCOG) yachting competition manager Glenn Bourke outlined the plan in Sydney at an Australian Yachting Federation and Yachting Association of NSW press conference to announce several successul Australian initiatives at the Brighton meeting:
* The choice of Sydney to host the ISAF World Youth Sailing Championships on Sydney Harbour in January 2000 -- the first international sporting event here in the Olympic Year.
* The selection of the Australian-designed Bethwaite 49er as the new High Performance Open Dinghy for Sydney 2000.
* The ISAF's unequivocal decision to adopt Bourke's plan to run three Olympic courses within the harbour and two outside Sydney Heads in what will be a grand spectacle of sailing in September 2000.

Bourke, a former three-time world Laser dinghy champion, Olympian, America's Cup and ocean racing sailor, put forward a plan that is practical and positive, providing excellent racing for competitors, spectacular viewing for spectators and public involvement in the medal presentations.

The courses for each of the 10 Olympic fleet racing disciplines are a radical change from traditional Olympic courses, and are designed around the shoreline and islands of the Harbour. Each course area has a choice of six windward directions to meet the wind patterns experienced on the harbour.
One course will be in the area between Athol Bight and Rushcutters Bay, a second in Rose Bay and north to the Sow and Pigs reef, and a third in The Sound of Port Jackson, just inside the Heads.

The offshore courses will be north and south of the Heads. The dinghy classes and sailboards will race within the Harbour, with the Tornado catamarans and Soling keelboats racing offshore, although the plan is to rotate the classes if conditions are suitable.
There is even an inshore storm course to take into account the variable weather conditions of September.
The Soling match racing finals will be sailed in the Farm Cove area, providing a magnificent viewing area for the public.
If the International Olympic Committee (IOC) agrees to an eleventh class for women's match racing, the finals of this discipline will also be held in Farm Cove.

JULIAN BETHWAITE, designer and builder of the 49er, told me on Thursday that since last week's announcement, he has received 85 overseas and 20 Australian orders for the new class, with some 140 already racing in the United States, Britain, Europe, Japan and Australia, with the main fleet at Woollahra Sailing Club in Sydney.
TERRA FIRMA TO DEFEND TITLE

Young Victorian computer systems company partners, DEAN WILSON and SCOTT CARLILE, have made a late entry into the fleet for the Telstra Sydney-to-Hobart with their IAIN MURRAY-designed 41-footer Terra Firma, the overall International Measurement System (IMS) winner of last year's race.

It seems they just forgot the closing date for applications to enter the big race, what with business commitments and supervising substantial changes to the keel of Terra Firma in preparation for her summer campaign.

Terra Firma will join a small but impressive line-up of Victorian yachts in this year's Sydney-Hobart, headed by JLW Chutzpah, the Hick-designed 35-footer owned by BRUCE TAYLOR, the Collins Street orthodontist and immediate past commodore of the Royal Yacht Club of Victoria.
JLW Chutzpah had notched up five successive IMS wins until last weekend, when she placed second in the Becks Regatta race.
The smaller Victorian contingent was expected as many of the locals are contesting the 25th annual race from Melbourne to Hobart, around Tasmania's rugged West Coast.

Not that the Terra Firma owners are the only ones who are slow with their applications to the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia (CYCA), with other late nominations dribbling into the club to take the fleet total close to 100 boats.
The real crunch comes on November 29, the deadline for paid-up entries.
Another late nomination is a second Mount Gay-30, Liklik, owned by Pittwater yachtsman DAVID FARRELL, joining RAY STONE's Razor's Edge.

Lightweight and smaller versions of the Whitbread-60 round-the-world racing yachts, Liklik and Razor's Edge have been designed by SCOTT JUTSON around the box design rules of this international offshore class.
SWISS CHALLENGE FOR AMERICA'S CUP

A Swiss challenge for the America's Cup in 2000 has been announced. While this may seem odd from a land-locked nation, we have seen Swiss participation in such events as the Whitbread Round-the-World Race and other major events and world one-design championships are regularly held on the Swiss lakes.
The Club Nautique de Morges on Lake Geneva will be the challenging club, supporting a Swiss-based organisation, FAST 2000, created by world famous yachtsmen MARC PAJOT and PIERRE FEHLMANN.

The inclusion of some of Europe's best sailors will strengthen the challenge, with triple Olympic gold medallist JOCHEN SCHUMANN of Germany and ENRICO CHIEFFI, the Italian world champion in the Star class, joining the team.
SCHUMANN was this week named ISAF World Sailor of the Year.

Sadly, only a few days after the announcement, the president of the FAST 2000 challenging club, JACQUES FAINI, was killed, with six of his business friends, in the crash of a private twin engine aircraft in central France.
FAINI had invested a lot of energy and enthusiasm in making the Swiss Challenge for the America's Cup a reality.
BRISBANE TO NOUMEA RACE FOR 1997
Many yacht owners who enjoy the challenge of long distance ocean racing were disappointed when the CYCA decided not to go ahead with next year's planned Sydney to Noumea Race.

They will be pleased to learn that the Queensland Cruising Yacht Club, in conjunction with the Cercle Nautique Caledonien, has picked up the ball and is planning a race from Brisbane to Noumea, starting on Saturday, September 6, 1997.
It is intended that there be a fully-crewed division requiring a minimum of four crew, but also a short-handed division with crew numbers restricted to two.
All yachts will be allocated a Performance Handicap Rating Factor and, dependant upon the numbers of entrants, there will be IMS and cruising categories.
TRANS-PACIFIC CHALLENGE IN 11-METRE ONE DESIGN CLASS
A trans-Pacific championship based on the famous AmAus Cup is to be revived following the completion of the Tarac Eleven-Metre One Design Australian championship on Sydney Harbour last weekend.
The seven race championship will be used as a guide to the selection of the four-yacht Australian team to be matched against rivals from San Francisco's St Francis Yacht Club later this season.
Eleven-Metre One Design class association officials have been negotiating with the Americans for some time for the revival of an AmAus Cup style series.
During the 1980s, an intense match-racing competition developed in the Six-Metre class between yachts representing the Royal Prince Alfred Yacht Club and the St Francis Yacht Club.

Now with the Eleven-Metre One Design class strongly established on San Francisco Bay, the Americans who won the last AmAus series have advised they are ready to send a team of class sailors to Australia for another showdown.
The Australians have accepted the challenge.
*Peter Campbell is editor of Offshore Yachting magazine.
